questions.problem:
$$ \{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)={x}^{2}(t)+2y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-3x(t)+{y}^{2}(t)\end{aligned} $$ Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the corresponding linearized system at the equilibrium point ${x}^{∗}=[0,\text{ }0]^{T}?$
${u}^{′}=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}} $\,\,u,\,$ where $u=x-{x}^{∗}$
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
questions.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2y \\ -3x+{y}^{2}\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}]
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2y)=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2y)=2 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-3x+{y}^{2})=-3,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-3x+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}2x & 2 \\ -3 & 2y\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}2(0) & 2 \\ -3 & 2(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -3 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, near the equilibrium, the nonlinear system is approximated by

$$
{u}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -3 & 0\end{aligned}]u,
$$

where the deviation vector is

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}].
$$

{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
questions.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}4x+{y}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}-5y\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}]
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x+{y}^{2})=4,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x+{y}^{2})=2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-5y)=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-5y)=-5\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2y \\ 2x & -5\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2(0) \\ 2(0) & -5\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, near the equilibrium, the nonlinear system is approximated by

$$
{u}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}]u,
$$

where the deviation vector is

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}].
$$

$$ \{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)={x}^{2}(t)+2y(t)-6 \\ {y}^{′}(t)=x(t)-3y(t)+{y}^{2}(t)\end{aligned} $$ Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the corresponding linearized system at the equilibrium point ${x}^{∗}=[2,\text{ }1]^{T}?$
${u}^{′}=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}} $\,\,u,\,$ where $u=x-{x}^{∗}$
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
questions.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2y-6 \\ x-3y+{y}^{2}\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}]
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2y-6)=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2y-6)=2 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x-3y+{y}^{2})=1,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x-3y+{y}^{2})=-3+2y\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}2x & 2 \\ 1 & 2y-3\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}2(2) & 2 \\ 1 & 2(1)-3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, near the equilibrium, the nonlinear system is approximated by

$$
{u}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]u,
$$

where the deviation vector is

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}x-2 \\ y-1\end{aligned}].
$$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=xy-{y}^{2}-1 \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+5\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the behavior of the system’s solutions near the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}={[2,\text{ }1]}^{T}?$

$\,$
The equilibrium is an  
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}xy-{y}^{2}-1 \\ -{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+5\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy-{y}^{2}-1)=y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy-{y}^{2}-1)=x-2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+5)=-2x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+5)=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have:

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}y & x-2y \\ -2x & -2y\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}(1) & 2-2(1) \\ -2(2) & -2(1)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -4 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that the matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), so the system is almost linear at ${x}^{∗}.$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 0 \\ -4 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(-2-\lambda ) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=-2,1.$

Finally, since we have two real eigenvalues with opposite signs, our equilibrium is an $\text{unstable}$ $\text{saddle}.$

\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2x(t)+y(t)+x(t)^{3} \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-2x(t)+y(t)^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the behavior of the system's solutions near the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[0,\text{ }0]^{T}?$

questions.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}2x+y+{x}^{3} \\ -2x+{y}^{3}\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}]
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =2+3{x}^{2},\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =1 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =-2,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =3{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}2+3{x}^{2} & 1 \\ -2 & 3{y}^{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[0,\text{ }0]^{T}$ to get

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}2+0 & 1 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 1 \\ -2 & -\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(-\lambda )+2 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=1\pm i.$

Since we have two complex eigenvalues with positive real parts, our equilibrium is an $\text{unstable}$ $\text{spiral source}.$
